utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated, we are resuming the hearing. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are the interpreters ready? Good morning, good morning everybody. Does Mr. Blaskic hear? Does the Defence, the Prosecutor, my colleagues? Then we can resume the hearing and hear the new witness, called in by the Prosecutor. Mr. Kehoe, before we have him brought in, this is a witness that you plan to ask him questions about how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say, your Honour, that it would probably run about two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As your colleagues did for your other colleagues, the judges would like you to go as directly as possible to those questions which are substantive for the Prosecution in the proceedings against General Blaskic. Now we can have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the witness is Elvir Ahmic. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you first give me your first name and your last name? Repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Elvir Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The usher is going to give you a statement which you are going to read, the statement you take before the judges. ELVIR AHMIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elvir Ahmic, you may be seated. You are before a Tribunal, before judges who are going to hear you, because the Prosecutor wanted you to be heard as part of a trial which is being conducted against General Blaskic for events which apparently you were witness to. You must speak without fear, you have nothing to be afraid of in front of the judges here. First you will have questions from the Prosecutor, who must have explained this to you, therefore I can ask you to relax. This is a trial and there is an accused, presumed to be innocent, which means that his guilt has not yet been proved. Then you must hear the Defence attorneys who will also ask you questions and then, of course, throughout the hearing or at the end, the judges reserve the right also to ask you questions. If you have anything at all that you need, any problem, do not hesitate to say so. We can now continue, or rather begin, the examination. Mr. Kehoe, you will be the one to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours. Good morning, Elvir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, how old are you now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, how old were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am being told that the French booth cannot hear you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The microphone is on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, everything is fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, you said you are now 18. How old were you on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In April 1993, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In what part of Ahmici did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you live in the area of the lower mosque or did you live in Gornji Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, near the lower mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In April 1993, who did you live with, who was in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was my father, my mother, my brother, a younger brother and a sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is the name of your younger brother and how old was he on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Semir Ahmic and he was eight years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your sister, what was her name and how old was she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Her name was Enisa Ahmic and she was four years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, let us move back to that day or the day before. Were you going to school in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where were you going to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the elementary school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your class, Elvir, did you have Bosnian Croats and Muslims and Serbs all in the same class?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After school, when you went home, or just after school generally, did you and your other friends, your Croat friends and Serb friends, play together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about football games? Did you play football games together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th April, we played without them, they did not come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But before 15th April, had you played football games very often with your Croat friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The football game was different on 15th April, was it not, because you said your Croat friends did not show up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, in addition to your Croat friends not showing up for the football game, did you notice any activity among the Croats in your neighbourhood on the afternoon of 15th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw my next door neighbours, they were sort of panicking, there was a lot of movement, they were moving around with their families. They were taking away their family members to Vitez and Busovaca and when they came back, they came back without their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So who was taken away and who came back? Were women and children taken away and the men came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the women and children were taken away and the men returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How long a period of time did this go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were at home that night from the 15th going into the morning of the 16th, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what happened on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you do that, Elvir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning of 16th April, my younger brother woke me up because he was awakened by the sound of shooting. In the meantime, my mother spoke to her father on the telephone, and I heard her father telling her to get ready to run, to flee, because the war had gun. She told him that we were all on our way. After this talk on the phone, she came into our room, and told us to get dressed and to seek shelter, so we got up and went into the hallway. When we reached the hallway, the entrance to our house was open. I stood there next to the door and my younger brother went off with my mother. It was quite by chance that I looked towards the door and I saw somebody's hand throwing into the house quite a large bomb. It fell close to me and it rolled off in the direction of my mother. My mother grabbed it into her right hand, and she tried to throw it out, but it went off in her hand and her hand was cut off, and this bomb killed her and my brother also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Elvir. You say the bomb killed your brother. Did it kill your mother at that point also, or did your mother live for a while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the explosion, she only suffered heavy injuries. She was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But that explosion killed your young brother Semir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I turned around towards them and I saw that my brother had been hit, but I did not know that he was dead until I checked for myself. Then I tried to put on my sweat suit, but next to my feet, I saw a bomb in front of me. However, it exploded, and I suffered light injuries all over my body. Then I ran away into my own room, I hid behind the door. However, a Croatian soldier came into the house and followed me into my room. He threw in another bomb. The bomb exploded and he came in and he started pushing the door towards me. When he saw that I was alive, he said -- he told me to come out of the room. I did, I came out, and the first thing he asked me was whether I had any matches, and "where is your father?", he said. I said that I did not know. He then asked me whether there was anybody else upstairs. I said there was not. Then he went upstairs and he threw two bombs and while he was upstairs, I picked up my younger sister and carried her into the cellar and I helped my mother to come down with us. My mother asked where my brother was and I said he was in the kitchen and that he was dead. She asked me to bring him over, and so I went to fetch him. When I came out of the cellar, I saw that the house was in flames and that my brother was in the middle of the fire, so I went back to the cellar and I said that he was in the kitchen, and the kitchen was burning already. Then she asked me to get him out of the kitchen, so that he would not burn. When I tried to do that, I could not, because there was a lot of smoke, so I took a deep breath and rushed through the flames to reach him. I grabbed him by his feet and dragged him into the hallway. I called my mother and sister, telling them to get out of the house, because it was no longer possible to stay there. Mummy was the first to walk out of the house, but at my neighbours, Husein Ahmic, there were four or five of them still there, Croatian soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, let me stop you there for a second. You mentioned that a Croatian soldier came into your house and threw the two bombs upstairs, and then you mentioned the Croatian soldiers outside. What type of soldiers were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my mother was hit by them again in the stomach, and she fell on her back, and she said to me that I should carry my brother to the outdoor kitchen that we had, but that kitchen was locked, so I carried him to the stable, and I left him there in a corner which we never used. Then I came back for my sister and I put her also in the trough and then I tried to help my mother because she was very badly wounded. When I saw her, she was already following us, she was crawling on her hands and feet, she was propping herself up with her broken right arm. I asked if I could help her and she said there was no need. I tried, but she did not want me to help her. She also got in and lay down next to my brother. Then she told me to look after my sister and to take the money which was in the house. Half an hour later, she passed away. My sister and I got up and we blocked the door so that it could not be opened. I took my sister back into the cow trough, and in the stable, we still had a cow and a lamb. I would lose consciousness repeatedly because I had lost a lot of blood. About midnight I came to, and I heard some soldiers who were there near the house, and one of them started pushing the door of the stable open --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, let me ask you a question before you go into the soldiers. You said that you fainted because you were losing a lot of blood. How many wounds did you have at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eighteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where were those wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All over my body, from my head to my heel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also said that when your mother went out of the house first that she was shot by one of the HVO soldiers. Did you see which soldier shot her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised only one of them, and his name was Andjelko Vidovic and his nickname was Acko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did you know Acko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Acko have any type of white band or any band at all around his left arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a white band on his left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the other soldiers that were with him also have bands on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. One of them had an orange band and the others had white bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, I just want to ask you a couple of questions about the soldier that came into your house the first time. Did you recognise that soldier, or was he disguised in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was painted over with black, some kind of black paint on his face, and he was carrying an automatic rifle with a double frame and another weapon on his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the weapon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: RPG.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, what was the weapon that he had on his back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a weapon for destroying carriers, personnel carriers or bunkers, a RPG.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that this soldier asked where your father was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know where your father was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was, on the evening of the 15th April, he was due to be in the patrol, but I was not sure whether he had left or whether he had stayed home. In any case, I did not see him that evening. I was not quite sure whether he was on patrol or whether he was hiding some place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about these patrols in Ahmici. What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their task was to patrol the village of Ahmici, to provide protection and security against the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these patrols part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did your father participate with some other men with these nightly patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that, just moving ahead, you said that you were in the barn at about midnight when you woke up. Tell the judges what happened when you woke up, what did you hear, what did you smell and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around midnight, I woke up, and I could feel that the roof of the barn was on fire and that there were some Croatian soldiers around the house. One of them tried to force the door open, but he could not, because it was blocked. Then he called his colleague by name, "Mirko, come here", he said, "I cannot open this door. Will you help me?" Then he came and they started forcing the door open. They managed, they succeeded and they opened the door, but not altogether, just far enough so as to be able to throw in a bomb through the opening. When they threw the bomb in, it went off and then they also pushed through their rifles and started shooting all over the shed. I put my hand over my sister's mouth and told her to keep quiet, that she must not say anything. When they stopped shooting, they peeped in and they saw my mother and my brother lying there, and they said, "we have killed a woman and child", and my mother and younger brother had already been dead before that. Then I am not quite sure, but their commander -- anyway they told him that in the stable there was still a cow and a lamb and he ordered them to get the cow and lamb out, so that they would not burn. They refused to do that, because they did not want to lead the cow and lamb out over dead bodies. And then he said, "all right, do whatever you want", and then they went round the back and broke a window and then they threw in one bomb and the cow immediately fell to the concrete. Because the bomb did not kill her, they fired another three or four bullets into her, into the cow, and then they also killed the lamb with their rifle. Then they later came by, bringing their colleagues to show them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about that, Elvir. What did they bring their colleagues to show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They showed them how, as if they had killed my brother and mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they bragging about it, or were they sad and upset about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were bragging about it, they were proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Through this shooting and the bombs, you and your sister were not hurt any further. How did you protect yourself in the barn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that, when we had just arrived in the stable, we lay in the concrete cow trough, which was on the ground, and that is how we were protected from the shelling, the bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that these were Croatian soldiers. When you say Croatian soldiers, are you talking about HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers did you see and hear around that barn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around ten or fifteen of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, after these HVO soldiers called their colleagues over to brag about killing your mother and your brother, what happened next? Did they make any calls on the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They used a Motorola to inform their command that by the lower mosque in Ahmici everything was slaughtered and killed, and that they were moving towards the upper mosque, towards Gornji Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had many Muslims fled towards Gornji Ahmici from lower Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a few of them had fled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you heard this radio communication about everybody slaughtered down in lower Ahmici and that they were heading towards upper Ahmici, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they left and I stayed on after them, I was still conscious. I got up to see what was going on around my house and I saw that many houses were on fire and that no one was there, none of the Muslim owners of these houses were there. After that, I returned to the cow trough and that is where I lost consciousness, and on 17th April, I woke up in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, before we talk about you waking up in the afternoon, the houses that you saw on fire, were they Muslim houses or were they Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said when you went back into the barn and you got back in the trough, you lost consciousness. Was your sister still with you, and what was your sister doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was terrified, and she did not move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your sister -- at this time Enisa was four years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move ahead on the 17th. You said that you lost consciousness early in the morning on the 17th and you woke up in the afternoon. Tell us what happened after you woke up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I regained consciousness, I got out of the stable, I took a ladder and I brought it into the stable. There was an opening on the roof, and I used the ladder to climb up to the top of the stable with my sister, and I left her up there, and I went back with the intention of going into the house and finding something to eat. My sister and I were very hungry, because we had not eaten anything for two days. I went to the house, but everything was still burning, it was too hot. I took a pair of slippers and I walked into the house, though. The lower floor had burned down, my room, but the bathroom, the bedroom and the staircase was still there. I walked into the bedroom, I took some clothing, money, and I started leaving the house. As I started leaving the house, I turned towards the staircase, accidentally, and I saw a body lying there. I wanted to go back to the stables, but our neighbour's house was set on fire then, and that drew my attention. I accidentally looked towards a house that was owned by a Bosnian Croat, and I saw the owner of that house standing there by his house. He was watching Gornji Ahmici, he was wearing a black uniform, his name was Ivo Papic. I was looking around my house, and I saw my neighbour Sejad Ahmic lying dead, and I saw Melisa Zec, who was around seven years old, I saw her lying by her dead mother. I called out to her and asked her to come with me. She did not want to, she just told me that she would not go away from her mother and that her mother was asleep. She said, "I do not want to leave my mother". I saw her mother, Hajrija Ahmic, and I realised she was dead, because she was just lying there and bleeding from the mouth, and from the stomach. Then I saw my neighbour, Husein Ahmic, lying in his yard. He was also dead. Then I asked Melisa Zec where her father was and she said, "he is over here", in a garden. I invited her to come with us towards Gornji Ahmici and she did not want to. I tried in vain to talk her into coming with us, but she wanted to stay with her dead mother. Then when I set out for Gornji Ahmici, I came across some soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, before we talk about your seeing some soldiers, you said that Melisa Zec was sitting next to her dead mother and that her father was nearby. Was her father dead as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you went into your house, you saw a body on the landing near the staircase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you think that person was dead at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I was surprised. How come another person in my house? But this was my schoolmate, whose name was Adnan Ahmic. He was wounded in the morning of April 16th by a Croat soldier, and during the cease-fire he came to see me in Zenica, and he told me about everything that had happened. According to his statement, he managed to dodge one Croatian soldier, but when he came across another one, this one told him that no one would get out of this place alive. He wounded him in his upper leg, and I wounded his foot. He remained lying there in the yard of the house owned by Mehmed Trako, who was also dead. Later, some soldiers came up to him, checking whether he was alive or dead, but he stopped breathing and they did not realise that he was alive. When they left, he got up and walked up to my house, because the roof of the stable and also of the room where there was fire wood, all of that was on fire, so he went up to there to get dry, because he was wet from the rain. When he got dry, he went upstairs in my house, because the upper floor was not burned down, but then he went, weakened, he remained lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he ultimately picked up by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after seven days, through the window, he saw UNPROFOR by the mosque in Donje Ahmici. He crawled up to them, they took him in, and took him to the hospital in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, you said when you woke up on the 17th that your neighbour's house was burning. Whose house was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the house of Mustafa Ahmic, and his old barn, and an old house that was owned by Abdulah Ahmic, and also his old barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see Abdulah Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not interpreted).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you saw the body of Ahmic Husein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How old was Ahmic Husein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Husein Ahmic was about 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You saw him dead on the afternoon of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just moving ahead, you asked Melisa to go with you and then you got your sister from the barn and you headed towards Gornji Ahmici. Why were you heading towards Gornji Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because up there I had my grandmother and my uncle. As we were walking we came across Croat soldiers who were members of the military police, the so-called Jokers. His leader called out to me and he asked me to come over. I stopped where I was, because I did not know what to do. He told me to come up to him, that they would not hurt me, that I should not be afraid, I started moving towards him and the first thing he asked me was, "how old are you?" , and I said that I was 14. In response, he said, "you are still a child". When I came up to him, there were other members of the military police with him, about 30 of them. He asked me, "where are you going?" I said that I wanted to go to my grandmother in Gornji Ahmici, and he said, "you cannot go to Gornji Ahmici, you will be killed by the HVO, because they cannot tell a child apart from a grown man". After that, he asked me, "would you like to go to Zenica and Travnik or wherever else you want to with UNPROFOR, or would you like to go with your own people?" I said, "I want to go with my own people", and he told five of his men, he ordered five of his men to take me to my own people, to Zume, where they were. We started going through the forest and I saw a woman who was lying on the ground, not far away from us, and I asked, "who is that woman?", and they told me, "that is none of your concern, just go on walking. Do not fall too so we will not have to carry you too". They were carrying my sister, you know. We came to the lower mosque, and they all sat on a fence that had not been finished yet, and they asked me, "is there anyone else over here who is still alive, that you know is still alive?", and I said, "in Ahmici, there is a little girl Melisa who is by my house". They went to pick her up and they brought her there. Then one of them used a Motorola to call the others who were at Zume, and he asked, "what shall we do with the three children we have up here? Shall we bring them there or should we take care of them?" The other person said that we should be brought there. We started walking, but one of them went to the other side, took the car of a neighbour of mine, and he rode off on his own, I do not know where. We continued on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, let me ask you a question before you continued on foot. He asked whether or not, the Joker that got on the Motorola, asked whether they should bring you and Melisa and your sister Enisa to Zume or "take care of them". What did you understand them to mean by the words "take care of them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that these men were part of the Jokers. Did you see a Joker insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had black insignia, on which it was inscribed in white letters, "Vojna Polizia", "military police", and down there "Jokers", "Jokeri" and in the middle there was a joker's head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just continuing, you began to walk towards Zume, after this Joker took your neighbour's car. Tell the judges what happened then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reached the house of Hasim Ahmic, and then someone started shooting at us. We ran away, we hid in a ditch before the shooting subsided, and then we went to Hasim Ahmic's house, where we hid. We spent some time there and some of them took my sister to the house of a Croatian schoolmate of mine, his name was Dario Cerkez. Then they also took Melisa there, and only one of them stayed behind with me. I had a bag with clothing in it, and he asked me to take the most important things out of my bag. I took money and gold, jewellery, all of it wrapped in a handkerchief. I took that out and started putting it into my pocket, and he asked me, "what is that?" I said, "money and jewellery", and he asked me, "how much do you have?" I said that I did not know. He took the money and counted it and told me not to tell anyone about it, that he and I would later agree on the money, which I accepted, because I had no other way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, how much money was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what my father told me, there was about 2,000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on. After he took this money, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We headed towards Cerkez's house and when we got there I saw many Croats standing with rifles, but they were not in uniform, they were in civilian clothes. Among them was another schoolmate of mine, Nenad Kristo, who had a semi-automatic rifle, and he was ordered to take the three of us to my people, where they were. Since this was quite far, if we went along roads, he headed across the meadows and the vegetable gardens. When we got there, many women and children could not recognise me, because I was all covered in blood, my face was covered in blood, and they told me to go and wash and then to come and get something to eat, so I did. We started eating, but we could not eat, because we were too hungry, so we just could not eat, we had no appetite so we left it. We spent the night there and on Sunday morning a Croatian soldier took us to the elementary school in Dubravica. He told us that we could not stay there, as there would be an exchange on Monday, that we should just spend the night there. When we got to the elementary school in Dubravica, there was there a brigade known as the Croatian Defence forces, the HOS, and the men were separated from the women and children, and they were put in a gym and the women and children in smaller class rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, you said that you went to the school where there were Croatian Defence force, that was HOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know whether HOS became Vitezovi prior to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you got into the Dubravica school, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there, I was told to go with the men to the gym, but a woman asked them not to separate me from my sister, because I only had her left. Then he approved and I went with my sister to where the women were. When we reached these class rooms, they gave us lunch, and they told us not to move around too much, and they told the women to determine our places, because the corridors in the elementary school were very dirty and that they had to be cleaned. Some women immediately started working. This happened on a daily basis. In the evening, many could not sleep, because there were the -- above us were the bedrooms, the dormitories, where they would sit, drink, break bottles and glasses, and one evening, two soldiers came. One was a member of the military police, because he had a white police force belt, and a white pistol holster. So they took out a woman and told her to find two young Muslim women that would suit them. The woman came back crying. She came back crying, and started to do what she was told to do. As nobody wanted to go, they came in again, took her out and said, "if you do not find them, then you will come with us". Then the woman came back and sat on a bed, telling the other women what she had been told. Then they came in again and took her out and they said to her, "if you do not find them now, we will come in and pick them ourselves". That is what actually happened. They came in, and with a lamp, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) An hour later she came back crying, telling the women that she had been raped in the car, and that she would never forgive them for this. A day or two later, two soldiers came, asking whether there were any wounded among the women and children and that they should get ready and that they would be taken to hospital. I and another woman went with them. We were put in a stolen car and taken towards the hospital, but we were not going towards the hospital in Travnik, but we went by Vitez, and we were taken to the basement of the youth centre, where there was a wartime improvised infirmary. There were many stretchers, blood-stained stretchers there, so this woman and I were given injections against infections and some other medicaments. Then we went back to the elementary school in Dubravica, and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, let me ask you a couple of questions. What kind of wounds did this woman have, that went to the clinic with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She had in the area of her right shoulder a very large wound with a fragment, a grenade fragment inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the HVO picked you up in a stolen car and took you to the clinic; how did you know that car was stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The car -- because they did not use keys to start it, but they used wires to get it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The soldiers that you said came in and selected the woman to take out and rape --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. (Pause). It had to do with the disclosure of a name which needs to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The soldiers that came in to take the people to the clinic, were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were soldiers of the Croatian Defence forces. They belonged to the units of the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, when you say HOS, are you talking about HOS and Vitezovi as the same organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The woman that was taken out to be raped, you said that one of those soldiers was a member of the military police, because you could describe him with the white belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see what the other soldier was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He only had a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, after you received this injection with the other woman at the clinic, you then were brought back to the Vitezovi school, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During that time you were at the Vitezovi school, did you see anybody, any soldiers that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Goran Godzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours. Elvir, at the break we were talking about you coming back to the school after you had finished in the clinic. What happened when you got back to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got back to the school, I went out into the corridor, and I saw through the window my teacher carrying an automatic rifle, and taking away Muslim men to do forced labour. His name was Goran Godzic. He was my music teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he have a uniform on, a HVO uniform on as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and he carried the insignia on his uniform of the Croatian Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Mr. Registrar, what is it that we hear, the works going on? It is a bit disturbing. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, after you saw Goran Godzic taking these men out for forced labour, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with them, he got into a small van which had on its window the flag, a white flag, with the sign of the Red Cross, and they were taken off for forced labour to dig trenches and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Goran Godzic put these men into a van with the Red Cross and took them out to do forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on, Elvir. Did anything happen after that before you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the UNPROFOR came, and they demanded from the command of the Croatian Defence forces that they should separate the wounded civilians, and that they should take them to hospital for treatment. The woman who went with me to the infirmary in Vitez, they tried to extract the fragment from her shoulder, but they could not do it. They could not do that there in the school, she needed to go to hospital. The Croatian Defence forces allowed that woman and her children to go to hospital when UNPROFOR asked that I should go to; they also allowed that, but without my sister. They insisted that my sister stayed behind and I would not accept that, so I stayed behind. When that woman was taken to the hospital in Zenica, and when the fragment was extracted she contacted my relatives and told them that I was in the elementary school in Dubravica, and my father's sister called the elementary school in Dubravica up on the phone, and asked them to talk to me, whether she could talk to me, and they let her. When I answered the phone, they did not know in Zenica whether I was alive and whether my brother was alive. They did not know who had survived. She told me that my father was alive and that he was in Zenica, not to worry, and that there would be an exchange soon, and that is the whole conversation we had. When May 1st came, the exchange was carried out on that day, and we were exchanged. I went to Zenica, where I met up with my father. And before the exchange, UNPROFOR asked for my permission to take Melisa Zec from the elementary school in Dubravica to her grandfather and grandmother, and I agreed, and after the truce was signed I learned that she reached her grandparents, that she is alive and well and that she is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Elvir, have you gone back to live in Ahmici since you were exchanged on 1st May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.text: Elvir, during your time when you grew up there, did you know most of the houses in your area that were owned by Muslims and that were owned by Croats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the Tribunal is not here in order to force the parties to move things forward quickly, any more than the parties wish to do.
